examples.name: Overview
examples.code:
const [returnsDisabled, setReturnsDisabled] = useState(false)

<Accordion type="single" collapsible defaultValue="shipping">
  <Accordion.Item value="shipping">
    <Accordion.Trigger>What are your shipping options?</Accordion.Trigger>
    <Accordion.Content>
      We offer standard (5–7 business days), express (2–3 days), and overnight shipping…
    </Accordion.Content>
  </Accordion.Item>
  <Accordion.Item value="returns" disabled={returnsDisabled}>
    <Accordion.Trigger>What is your return policy?</Accordion.Trigger>
    <Accordion.Content>Returns are accepted within 30 days of delivery…</Accordion.Content>
  </Accordion.Item>
  <Accordion.Item value="support">
    <Accordion.Trigger>How can I contact customer support?</Accordion.Trigger>
    <Accordion.Content>Reach us by email, live chat, or phone Monday–Friday…</Accordion.Content>
  </Accordion.Item>
</Accordion>
examples.details: Compose with Accordion.Item, Accordion.Trigger, and Accordion.Content. Built on Radix Accordion, so the primitive handles keyboard navigation, focus management, and WAI-ARIA semantics. On a phone an item reads as an iOS 27.2 DisclosureGroup in an inset grouped list: a 52px row with its title at 17/22 regular and a chevron in the label color that points to the end and turns down when the item opens. The chevron is 21px and ends 1px past the title's margin, where iOS draws it. The content is a row under the title, 17/22 in the label color, 20px in from it, with a separator above it across the row; under an open item the separator starts where the content does, as under the last row a group holds. Set type to multiple when readers can keep several sections open at once: settings pages, long FAQs, step-by-step references. A single accordion with collapsible lets readers close the open item; without it one item is always open. card composes the accordion inside Card, the most common landing-page FAQ pattern; on a phone the card is a section of the grouped list. The returnsDisabled control disables only the return-policy item. It remains visible and keeps its open state, while keyboard navigation skips its trigger.

components.name: Alert
components.description: Inline message for notices and warnings, with semantic colors, a title, a description and actions.

props.name: title
props.description: Title displayed in the alert

props.name: description
props.description: Description text

props.name: actions
props.description: Actions (for example buttons)

props.name: actionsPlacement
props.description: Placement of actions; automatic from sizing when unset

props.name: mobileActions
props.description: At 767px and below: 50px capsules as in an iOS tip, or the buttons at their own size, for an alert inside a block of its own buttons

props.name: actionsClassName
props.description: Class applied to the actions container

props.name: color
props.description: Color scheme

props.name: variant
props.description: Style variant

props.name: indicator
props.description: Custom indicator or false to hide

props.name: onDismiss
props.description: Shows the dismiss button when set

props.name: banner
props.description: Full-width strip: square corners, lines above and below only

props.name: className
props.description: Class applied to the alert container

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: color and variant style the alert. It shows a title, a description or both; each takes text or nodes, such as a <TextLink color="currentcolor"> to a status page. It has an indicator icon by default, chosen from its color: an icon in indicator replaces it, and indicator={'{false}'} hides it. actions takes buttons or other nodes. They are placed automatically, at the end or, when they take more than a third of the alert's width, under the message, unless actionsPlacement is 'end' or 'bottom'. onDismiss adds a Dismiss button in the alert's chrome; for a dismissible notice, labeled buttons in actions are the suggested approach. A solid alert is for a message alone: buttons, Dismiss among them, do not read on its color, so this preview offers them on soft and outline alerts. Use banner for a full-width strip across the top or bottom of a page or panel (offline, read-only, a new version): it drops the rounded corners and keeps only the lines above and below. On a phone an alert takes the shape and text of an iOS tip (TipKit), the system's message inside a screen: 26px corners (a banner stays square), the title at 17/22 semibold and the description at 15/20, and a close button in its corner instead of Dismiss. A title or a description alone stands its first line on the middle of the icon. A soft or outline alert turns gray, as a tip is: the secondary fill with no border, the title in the text color and the description in the secondary label, and only its icon keeps the alert's color (a neutral alert's icon is the secondary label); a solid alert keeps its color. Its actions always stand under the message as 50px capsules side by side, so actionsPlacement is a desktop setting. With mobileActions="own" the actions keep the size you give the buttons, for an alert inside a block of its own buttons, and they start where the text starts.

props.description: Absolute URL for image avatar

props.name: Icon
props.description: Icon component for icon avatar

props.name: size
props.description: Width and height in pixels

props.name: color
props.description: Semantic color for text/icon avatar

props.name: variant
props.description: Style variant

props.name: overflowCount
props.description: Show overflow count (e.g. +9)

props.name: className
props.description: Applied to the avatar root

props.name: onClick
props.description: Makes avatar interactive (renders a button)

props.name: onPointerDown
props.description: Makes avatar interactive (renders a button)

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: An avatar shows one of four things. Without other props it shows the first letter of name. With imageUrl, an absolute URL, it shows the photo with a soft fade once it loads, and the initial if it fails. With Icon, an icon component such as Robot from @plexui/ui/components/Icon, it shows the icon; name is not shown, and only names the avatar when it is a button. With overflowCount it shows the count, formatted and scaled to fit. size sets the width and height in pixels, and the initial, icon and count scale with it. color and variant style every avatar except a loaded photo, which covers them. Avatars are fully rounded by default; a Tailwind rounding class in className overrides that. An onClick (or onPointerDown) handler makes the avatar a button with interaction styles and its name as the accessible name.

examples.name: Overview
examples.code:

examples.details: Breadcrumb renders a nav landmark named "Breadcrumb" around an ordered list. An item with href is a link (internal paths use the linkComponent of PlexUIProvider, such as your router's link); the current item is plain text marked aria-current="page". iOS has no breadcrumb, a phone screen goes back with the back button of its Toolbar. A trail kept on a phone takes the 15/20 text of iOS and gives each link a 44px touch target. A small chevron stands between items by default; pass any node to separator, such as a slash for file paths. Separators are hidden from assistive technology. Use size="sm" for a trail above a compact header; the default md sits above a page title. On a phone both sizes take the same text, so the size setting is desktop only.

components.name: Button Group
components.description: Join buttons into a single visual unit for toolbars, steppers, split buttons and search affordances.

props.name: orientation
props.description: Direction of the joined items

props.name: mobileMaterial
props.description: Phone surface with touch.css: "glass" makes the group one glass capsule outside a Toolbar, and a group that holds a field comes apart into glass shapes; "flat" keeps the joined buttons in one

props.name: className
props.description: Applied to the root <div>

examples.name: Overview
examples.code:
const [size, setSize] = useState("sm")

// Desktop
<ButtonGroup>
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="Go back">
    <ArrowLeftSm />
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size}>Pin</Button>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size}>Tag</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size}>Bookmark</Button>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="More options">
    <DotsHorizontal />
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
</ButtonGroup>

// Phone: the bars of a note
<Page>
<Toolbar>
  <Toolbar.Leading>
    <NavigationButton action="back" />
  </Toolbar.Leading>
  <Toolbar.Trailing>
    <ButtonGroup aria-label="Note actions">
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Pin"><Pin /></Button>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Tag"><Tag /></Button>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="More"><DotsHorizontal /></Button>
    </ButtonGroup>
  </Toolbar.Trailing>
</Toolbar>
<Page.Content>…</Page.Content>
<Toolbar placement="bottom">
  <Toolbar.Leading>
    <ButtonGroup aria-label="Editing tools">
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Checklist"><NotebookCheck /></Button>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Attach"><Clip /></Button>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="Markup"><Pens /></Button>
    </ButtonGroup>
  </Toolbar.Leading>
  <Toolbar.Trailing>
    <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="New note"><PencilSquare /></Button>
  </Toolbar.Trailing>
</Toolbar>
</Page>
examples.details: Wraps any row of controls (Button, Input, Popover.Trigger, etc.) and removes the shared border so they read as one unit. On a phone with touch.css a group of buttons in a Toolbar is the Button Group of iOS: one glass capsule holding its buttons, the same as Toolbar.Group. mobileMaterial="glass" asks for the capsule outside a toolbar, for controls that float over the content. iOS has no joined buttons in the content, so a group there keeps its joined look at the touch sizes. A field among glass buttons comes apart from them, each a glass shape of its own, as the composer of iOS Messages. The Phone view of each example shows the group where iOS puts it, in a bar or floating at the bottom of the screen, or the screen iOS builds where it has no such group. Set size on every Button inside the group so corner radii match; the size setting here sets all of them. Mix icon-only (uniform) with text buttons; each child keeps its own padding. Place a ButtonGroup inside a ButtonGroup to make sub-groups, as Back, Pin and Tag, Bookmark and More here, or a pager's pages beside its arrows: the outer group sets a gap between them (--button-group-nested-gap, 8px) and each sub-group stays joined. On a phone with touch.css a group in the content keeps one height. Beside text buttons its icon-only buttons take the heights of the iOS small (28px, sm) and medium (34px, md and lg) buttons; a group of icon-only buttons keeps their 44px, and beside a text field or a select every button takes the field's 44px. Joined segments have no iOS control of their own. On a phone the example is the bars of a note, as in iOS Notes: Back alone, the note's actions in one glass capsule on top, the editing tools in one at the bottom beside New Note. A ButtonGroup in a Toolbar is that capsule, as iOS 27.2 sets it: 44px buttons 10px apart in a 154px capsule on top, 48px ones 8px apart in a 164px capsule at the bottom, the symbols in the primary label color. Groups side by side stand apart as the bar's items do. The bar sets its buttons' size, so the phone view leaves out the size control.

examples.name: Orientation
examples.code:
const [size, setSize] = useState("sm")

// Desktop
<ButtonGroup orientation="vertical" aria-label="Zoom controls">
<Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="Zoom in">
  <PlusSm />
</Button>
<Button variant="outline" color="secondary" size={size} uniform aria-label="Zoom out">
  <Minus />
</Button>
</ButtonGroup>

// Phone: zoom controls over a canvas
<ButtonGroup orientation="vertical" mobileMaterial="glass" aria-label="Zoom controls" className="absolute top-2 right-4">
<Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill iconSize="sm" aria-label="Zoom in"><PlusLg /></Button>
<Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill iconSize="sm" aria-label="Zoom out"><MinusLg /></Button>
</ButtonGroup>
examples.details: Pass orientation="vertical" to stack the buttons, useful for + / − steppers, zoom controls, or any vertical toolbar. On a phone the example is zoom controls floating over a canvas, as map controls do: with mobileMaterial="glass" the group is the vertical Button Group of the iOS 27 kit, a 48px wide capsule of 48px buttons 6px apart. Each button takes its share of the gap and the padding, so its pressed shape fills its part of the capsule and the first and last are as round as its ends. A phone takes the large plus and minus (PlusLg, MinusLg) with iconSize="sm", the plus of an iOS 27.2 bar: about 18px of ink with a 2px stroke. In the content a group of icon-only buttons keeps their 44px at each size, so the phone view leaves out the size control.

examples.name: Input group
examples.code:
const [size, setSize] = useState("sm")
const [voiceEnabled, setVoiceEnabled] = useState(false)

// Desktop
<ButtonGroup style={{ width: "100%", maxWidth: 280 }}>
<ButtonGroup>
  <Button variant="outline" color="secondary" pill size={size} uniform aria-label="Add attachment">
    <Plus />
  </Button>
</ButtonGroup>
<ButtonGroup>
  <Input
    pill
    size={size}
    placeholder={voiceEnabled ? "Recording your idea…" : "Describe a component…"}
    disabled={voiceEnabled}
    endAdornment={
      <Input.AdornmentButton
        color={voiceEnabled ? "caution" : undefined}
        aria-label="Toggle voice mode"
        aria-pressed={voiceEnabled}
        onClick={() => setVoiceEnabled((prev) => !prev)}
      >
        <Mic />
      </Input.AdornmentButton>
    }
  />
</ButtonGroup>
</ButtonGroup>

// Phone: the composer at the bottom of the screen
<Page>
<Toolbar>
  <Toolbar.Title>New Message</Toolbar.Title>
  <Toolbar.Trailing>
    <NavigationButton action="close" />
  </Toolbar.Trailing>
</Toolbar>
<Page.Content>…</Page.Content>
<Page.Footer>
  <ButtonGroup mobileMaterial="glass" aria-label="Message">
    <ButtonGroup>
      <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill iconSize="sm" aria-label="Add attachment"><PlusLg /></Button>
    </ButtonGroup>
    <ButtonGroup>
      <Input pill aria-label="Message" placeholder="Text Message" endAdornment={…} />
    </ButtonGroup>
  </ButtonGroup>
</Page.Footer>
</Page>
examples.details: Richer composition for message composers: wrap each slot (leading action, flexible Input) in its own ButtonGroup so the outer group inserts a gap between them. The voice toggle rides inside the input via endAdornment. Use Input.AdornmentButton: it sizes off the input's own size token so the button stays concentric with the pill at every size. On a phone the example is the composer of iOS Messages at the bottom of the screen. With mobileMaterial="glass" a group that holds a field comes apart: the plus is a 40px glass circle with the large plus (PlusLg, iconSize="sm") and the field a 40px glass capsule with 16px gutters and 17px text, 12px apart, as iOS 27.2 sets them. The voice button inside the field keeps its 44px target without growing the field. The group sets the sizes, so the phone view leaves out the size control.

examples.code: const [size, setSize] = useState("sm") // Desktop Generate a component Describe what to build in plain English.
examples.details: Same split-button shape, but the trailing trigger opens a Popover instead of a menu, useful for richer panels (prompt composers, notification preferences, link previews). On a phone, as the Dropdown menu, the action and More are symbols in one glass capsule of the top bar. examples.name: Overview
examples.details: One button with every setting. color and variant style it: eight semantic colors, each solid, soft, outline or ghost. On a phone with touch.css iOS draws solid as Filled, soft as Tinted, or Gray in secondary, and ghost as Plain; outline is Plex UI's own. The Phone preview offers the colors of iOS buttons: accent (primary), gray (secondary) and destructive (danger). size sets the control height, and gutterSize the horizontal padding. Each size provides default values for gutterSize and iconSize, as well as font-size; each can be overridden on its own. pill rounds the corners fully and adds horizontal gutter. Button shares the unified 9-step size scale with Input, Select, SelectControl and SegmentedControl. On a phone with touch.css a button takes one of the three heights of iOS buttons: small 28 (3xs to sm), medium 34 (md, lg) and large 50 (xl to 3xl), always a capsule: the small one with a 15px label and 10px gutters, the medium and large ones with a 17px label and 12 and 20px gutters, as iOS 27.2 sets them, so the Phone preview offers sm, md and xl and neither pill nor gutterSize. Without size a button is md, the medium one; a screen's actions take xl. The label is Medium (510) and Regular on a ghost button, as the iOS 27 kit sets its buttons on glass and its plain ones, and as Apple's apps set a filled action apart from a plain one. Icons are children: icon here puts one before the label, after it, or alone, when the button needs an aria-label. Their size is automatic, from size, unless iconSize sets it. For a button of an icon alone, uniform makes it square and ignores gutterSize; with pill it is a circle. On a desktop a smaller gutterSize than size makes a well-sized icon button that is not exactly square. On a phone with touch.css the icon follows the three iOS sizes unless iconSize is set: 3xs to sm show the 18px icon and md to 3xl the 20px one, as iOS sets a button's symbol at the size of its label (15 and 17px). A button of an icon alone is the kit's symbol button, a circle as tall as a text button of its size, 28, 34 or 50px, with or without uniform, and gutterSize does not change it, so the Phone preview does not offer uniform. A toolbar, the bars of Page and Dialog, a ButtonGroup of uniform buttons alone and a button beside a field keep the 44px circle of a bar button in the kit (50px at 3xl). Between an icon and a label a button leaves 8px at every size, as iOS 27.2 does. block makes the button as wide as its container, a 290px column here. On a phone a screen's main action is the large button as wide as the screen, xl and block; the example stands at the top of the screen, next to its controls. disabled disables the button visually and accessibly. loading shows a spinner and prevents interaction through its default inert state; the controls show these props and start no asynchronous action. inert blocks a button without any visual change: it applies disabled for accessibility, and the look of a disabled button comes only from [data-disabled]. On a phone a disabled button labels in the tertiary label of iOS on the gray of a gray button, as iOS 27.2 draws a disabled filled or gray button; a ghost one has no fill, an outline one keeps its border with no fill, and a glass one keeps the glass. A loading button shows the iOS spinner there, 18px in the small button and 20px in the medium and large ones. selected shows that a button is open or selected; each variant shows it its own way. Menu and Popover set it on their trigger while open, through [aria-expanded="true"] or [data-state="open"]. iOS buttons show no selected state, so the Phone preview does not offer it; the prop still applies there.

A link opens in a new tab with a modifier click, shows its address, and is announced as a link. It takes the settings of the Overview but uniform, loading and selected, and on a phone it is the same iOS button. A relative href or to goes through the LinkComponent configured on PlexUIProvider, so your router handles navigation and prefetching (see ButtonLink below). An absolute URL, or external, renders an <a> with target="_blank" and rel="noopener noreferrer"; set external when a link is not identified on its own. The example's arrow then points up and out, as an external link's does. disabled disables the link visually and accessibly: it renders a span[role="link"], and onClick handlers are not bound.

Pass checked="indeterminate", or defaultChecked="indeterminate", for a partly selected state: a "select all" box whose items are only partly checked, as in Group with select all. solid (default) fills the box; ghost renders only the checkmark, in the text color, without a border or background, for subtle inline selections or task lists. pill rounds the box (border-radius: full): the solid fill, and on a ghost box its hover tint and focus ring. examples.name: Overview
examples.details: On Phone, put a date picker in a row of a FieldGroup, as the Forms: Settings do. In the row its trigger is the compact date of iOS: a capsule with the date that opens the calendar, 8px under it and, on a screen 392px wide or wider, 32px from its edge, as iOS 27.2 opens it; with a time format the date and the time are two capsules 8px apart, as Calendar shows an event's start. The row's capsule is its frame and sets its height, insets and type, and iOS opens the calendar under the row, so the Phone previews leave out the variant, size, pill, block, icon, date format and placement controls, and set {'triggerShowIcon={false}'} and the date as iOS writes it, "MMM d, yyyy". To type a date instead, put a Date Input in the row. Pass the date (a luxon DateTime, or null) as value and update it in onChange. showTime adds hour and minute fields under the calendar, which then stays open after a date is picked so the time can be set; the arrow keys step the field they are in. triggerTimeFormat writes the time after the date as a part of its own: on Phone, in a row, the date and the time are two capsules, as iOS shows an event's start. Without it, a showTime trigger writes "MM/dd/yy HH:mm" unless you set triggerDateFormat. captionLayout="dropdown" adds month and year dropdowns beside the arrows, for a date of birth or a date years away; yearRange sets their years (the last 120 by default); with min or max the years are those they allow, so here it is offered without limits. min and max limit the dates that can be picked: here 30 days either side of today, or up to today for a date of birth. Equal bounds leave one day.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: On Phone, put a date range picker in a row of a FieldGroup, as the Forms: Settings do. In the row the range and its up-down chevrons end at the row's edge, as a pop-up, and open the calendar. The row is its frame and sets its height, insets and type, so the Phone preview leaves out the variant, size, pill, block, clearable, icon, date format and placement controls, sets {'triggerShowIcon={false}'}, shows short dates (triggerDateFormat="MMM d") and None when there is no range. In a row the month of a month stepper keeps the width of the longest month, so its arrows stay put when the month changes. Pass the range ([start, end] luxon DateTimes, or null) as value and update it in onChange. triggerStepperUnit="month" adds a month stepper to the trigger: when the range is a whole month, the trigger shows the month with arrows to the previous and the next one. The shortcuts array offers quick ranges. When a shortcut is selected, its label is shown in the trigger and onChange receives that shortcut as its second argument. Each shortcut has a label and a getDateRange() function; here Today, Yesterday, Last 7 days and Last 30 days. A shortcut whose range falls outside min and max, or is longer than maxRangeDays, is disabled. The calendar doesn't show shortcuts below the md breakpoint. On a phone, offer them in a row of their own, as iOS settings offer presets: a Period row with a Select of the shortcut labels above the Dates row, which reads Custom when the dates match no shortcut. min and max limit the dates that can be picked: here the last 30 days up to today. maxRangeDays limits the length of the range. weekStartsOn sets the day each week of the calendar starts on, from 0 (Sunday) to 6 (Saturday).

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: At 767px and below a dialog is one of the two modal views of iOS. mobileVariant="alert" (or mobilePlacement="center") presents a compact centered glass alert, a confirmation or a request for one short value, with its actions side by side, or stacked from three, and no close icon. Any other dialog is a Sheet, the default, for forms and details: it opens at the bottom with a leading Close button and a centered title, and without a grabber, as iOS 27.2 draws one only on a sheet that changes height. Both variants preserve the desktop appearance. Two alert actions stand side by side and wrap onto separate rows when their labels need more space; three or more stack, as on iOS. Put long sheet content in Dialog.Body to keep the header and actions visible while the body scrolls. On a phone a dialog is one of the two modal views of iOS: an Alert (mobileVariant="alert"), a short question with its answers, or a Sheet, which it is by default (see Placement). The alert takes what the iOS 27 kit and UIAlertController offer. One, two or three actions: two stand side by side with Cancel first, and three or more stack in their order with Cancel last, as iOS sets them. Dialog.Footer mobileLayout="stacked" stacks two, for long labels. The main action is preferred (solid: the accent fill on a phone), plain (soft), or destructive (color="danger": a red label on the alert's fill on a phone). A title without a message stands centered. A field asks for one short value: a 48px capsule on a phone, its text selected when the alert opens, and Rename unavailable while it is empty. Label actions in title case, as iOS does.

examples.details: An empty message is made of parts, each optional: an icon, a title, a description and an action row. It needs a title or a description, so this preview offers description with a title; the description takes text or nodes, such as a search term in font-semibold. color on EmptyMessage.Icon and on EmptyMessage.Title shows the intent of the message, such as danger on both for an error (a missing permission) or warning on the icon for a notice (a feature in beta); the description keeps its own color. fill sizes the message to its parent: static takes the full width and height, absolute covers a positioned parent, and none applies no sizing, for a container that sets the height (a list with no results). Use size="sm" for an empty panel, card section or list: a smaller title, tighter spacing, no minimum width and a small icon badge; in a message of the default size the icon takes its own size. align="start" left-aligns the message, for an empty state under a section heading: a single line such as "No tags added" reads with the heading above it. The action row takes buttons, or a TextLink with className="text-sm" on the row. On a phone a message of the default size is iOS's ContentUnavailableView: the symbol bare, with no circle, in the secondary label, a 20px bold title right over a 17px description, and the block centred in the free space, whether it fills a screen or not. Its actions stand under the text, each at its own width, one under the other: a small capsule, then a plain button for a second action. examples.details: Field wraps a form control with a label, a description and an error message, and links them: the label's htmlFor, aria-describedby and aria-invalid reach the control. required adds an asterisk after the label; it is visual only, so give the control its own required for form validation. The layout control puts the label in its four places: above: the default, orientation="vertical". columns: orientation="horizontal", every value starting at one column. end: row, one line of a FieldGroup with the value at its end. A framed field is a pill there and takes --field-row-control-width, as its width cannot follow what is typed; pill={'{false}'} on the control keeps the rounded box. hidden: hideLabel. The label still names the control for screen readers; the placeholder shows what to type, and a description moves under the field. On Phone a field is always a cell of a FieldGroup on the grouped background, as in an iOS form, in the same four places: the label above its value (row orientation="vertical"), values in one column (FieldGroup columns), the value at the end of the row, or the placeholder alone (row hideLabel), its value starting at the row's edge. On Android a text field with its label above is a field of an input card, its label standing in the empty field and floating over the value, with a line under the field (Card of fields), and a placeholder-only cell stays a hint cell. The row is the field's frame, so a framed or soft field loses its frame. The error stands inside the cell, under the value. The words that explain a field go in the group's footer, and a required field says so in its placeholder, as iOS account forms do. A disabled text field dims only its value, as iOS shows a value that cannot be changed; a row unavailable as a whole takes data-disabled on the Field, which dims its label too; a row with a disabled checkbox, radio, switch or picker dims whole. A one-time code is the exception: OTPInput keeps its own digit cells on the screen, outside a group, as in Verify email. labelAction holds a link or a small control that acts on the field, at the end of the label row: a password reset, a template switch, a "Replace" link. It takes the label's font size. On Phone a row has no label line to hold it: the link stands under the group in the rows' text, as under the Apple Account sign-in. A group's footer is a footnote, for words to read. Here it is offered for a label above the field or in its column. The label and description scale with the child control: Field reads the control's size, so {''} gets a lg label without repeating it. Pass size to Field to set the label size yourself, or when the child is a render prop. Outside a row, with touch.css a text field is 44px from 3xs to 2xl and 50px at 3xl, with the 17px text of iOS. size, pill and opticallyAlign are the web's: on Phone a row sets the field's height, insets and type, and has no frame to align. opticallyAlign: "start" applies a negative margin on the child control, aligning its text with the surrounding content. Works with pill inputs. The label, description, and error message stay at the container edge while the control extends past it.

components.name: Float Input
components.description: Text input whose label floats above its value, with helper and error text and a multi-line variant.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: On Phone each field is a cell of a FieldGroup on the grouped background, and its placeholder names it: an Input, a Textarea or a Select in a Field row hideLabel, as the Forms: Settings do. On iOS a label does not float: iOS has no floating label, and the label stays for screen readers. On Android these cells stay hint cells; a row that shows its label over the value floats it instead (see Card of fields). A description goes in the group's footer, and an error stands inside the cell. The Phone previews show those cells; where the label rests and the shape of the field are desktop settings, and the Label inside example has no Phone view. Two things set the type: where the label rests (labelPlacement: on the border, or inside the box with the value under it), and the shape of the field. An empty field shows the label as a placeholder, so the difference appears once it has a value or the focus. pill={'{false}'} takes the rounded box of Input and Select with the label on the border; inside always takes the rounded box, so pill is offered only with the label on the border. Text fields, textareas and selects take both settings the same way. Both floating fields follow the same two tokens, so a form can set its radius and gutter in one place. Choose Empty or Filled to replace the value with a preset. The other controls preserve your text. Invalid and errorMessage demonstrate visual states, not email validation. An error message also marks the field invalid, so invalid is offered only without one; when both messages are enabled, the error appears before the description. Read-only text can still be selected and copied. onClear shows a built-in clear button: it appears when the field has a value and is not disabled or read-only, and focus returns to the field. On Phone the field is a cell named by its placeholder, and the cell is the frame, so labelPlacement and pill are desktop settings. The description goes in the group's footer and the error stands inside the cell. A cell has no frame to color, so invalid alone is desktop only.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: An index bar takes people through a long list that is sorted by its titles, such as countries or contacts, as the iOS section index does: a letter for each section down the trailing edge, and a press or a drag on a letter shows its section. Give a list one only when it is long and its sections are its letters. A desktop list has no index, so the bar renders under 768px only. The example shows the phone view. Put the bar in a Page, or in any positioned container that holds the list: it runs down the trailing edge, centred between the bars of a Page (or the safe areas), as iOS centres its index, its letters semibold, 13.79px apart and centred about 7.4px from the edge, where iOS 27.2 centres its own, in the info color, as iOS 27.2 draws its index and its tint. A drag highlights nothing, as on iOS. The rows keep the margins of the list, and the letters sit in the trailing one, as in Contacts. A press shows the section of the letter under the finger, and a drag moves through the sections letter by letter; onSelect receives the title and its index, and the list scrolls itself there. Where the letters do not fit, as in a short sheet, every other letter gives way to a dot, as UIKit's index does, and a drag over a dot still reaches the letters behind it.

components.name: Indicators
components.description: "Loading and progress indicators: spinners, determinate progress rings and animated dots."

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: indicator picks one of the three. LoadingIndicator is a spinner for general loading states. It takes the surrounding font-size and text color by default; size and strokeWidth set its size and stroke in pixels, a text class such as text-danger (or --indicator-color) colors it, and --indicator-rotate-duration sets the time of one turn. On a desktop it is a turning ring. With the optional touch stylesheet it is the iOS 27 spinner of eight rounded spokes: 20px by default, also inside a field (an Input adornment, an InputGroup addon or a SelectControl, through --control-indicator-size); up to 16px it takes the Small spokes and from 28px the Large ones. A strokeWidth replaces the spokes' widths, so the Phone view leaves it unset. CircularProgress is a progress ring. Without progress it simulates progress over maxDuration milliseconds, and done fills the ring and ends the simulation; this preview sets it every 4 seconds to start over. progress, from 0 to 100, shows a fixed value instead. size and strokeWidth (at most 4) size the ring, and trackColor and trackActiveColor color its track and its progress. LoadingDots shows typing progress with staggered pulsing dots in the current text color.

On Phone, an input group is the value of a row in a FieldGroup, as the Weight row of the Forms: Settings: the row's label names it, its prefix, unit, menu or button sits in the row, and the row is its frame. With a prefix the group takes columns, so the value starts at the column; without one the value ends at the row's edge with its unit or menu after it, as iOS writes "72 kg". A block addon turns the group into rows, so keep the other content of such a group inside its block addons, as the Textarea example does. Place addons after the control in the markup so the tab order starts with the field; align handles the visual position. loading shows a LoadingIndicator in an addon while a value is searched, checked or saved. On Phone the row is the frame: a group in a row keeps the default outline, which the row draws without a border, and the row sets its height (with touch.css 3xs to xl are all 44px; the iOS 26 field is one 52px row), so size, variant, pill and align stay on the desktop. The row places the value at its end, or, with columns, at one column shared by the group's rows; inline addons stay in the row, a block-start text becomes the row's label and a block-end text the group's footer. examples.name: Overview
examples.details: On Phone, put an input in a row of a FieldGroup, as the Forms: Settings do. Use variant to stylize the input. ghost has no border and no fill, for a field its container already frames, such as the search line at the top of a dialog; it still turns red when invalid. size sets the control height and gives a gutterSize (the horizontal padding) and a font-size, each of which can be overridden; Input shares the 9-step size scale with Button, Select, SelectControl and SegmentedControl, so adjacent controls of one size line up. pill rounds it fully. startAdornment puts content before the value, such as a prefix or a search icon, and endAdornment after it, such as a character counter. gutterSize sets the space at the edges (a negative margin on the adornment, such as -ml-2, fine-tunes it), and gap on the container the space between the adornment and the value. onClear shows a built-in clear button while the input has a value and is not disabled or read-only; clicking it keeps focus in the input. opticallyAlign ("start" or "end") offsets the gutter so the text lines up with the content around it, here the label; on a Field it is forwarded to its control. autoSelect selects all the text, useful with copy actions; it acts when toggled and leaves the selection free to change. Autofill extensions are prevented by default; allowAutofillExtensions lets them in, and a name or type="password" turns it on by default. readOnly keeps the value and hides the clear button. disabled greys the input out and blocks interaction. invalid marks it invalid, with [data-invalid] on the container; you decide how the state is removed (onFocus, onChange, an onSubmit handler). On Phone the row is the frame and sets the height, insets and type, so the input takes no variant, size, gutterSize, pill or opticallyAlign; with touch.css the 3xs to xl sizes are all 44px. The value stands at the end of the row, at one column for the whole group with FieldGroup columns, or under the label with orientation="vertical", where it is ghost. A start adornment is a prefix of the value and trailing text-secondary text takes the row's accessory color; the clear button is the filled circle of an iOS text field, shown only while the value is being edited, and a long value stops 6px before it. An error is the row's errorMessage under it. Browser autofill extensions are a desktop matter: on iOS autofill comes from the system above the keyboard. An Input in a Toolbar takes the bar's search field, and one with type="search" at the top of the content is the same glass field under a large title.

Put the rows in a FieldGroup: each is a row of the group, so its separators, corners and hover follow the card, and its height is the row's 52px, its words where a row's label starts (20px on a phone). A value too long to stand beside the label on one line goes under it with valuePlacement="auto", at the full width of the text, and a description under the value, as Calendar sets a long value (below puts it there always). examples.details: A page control shows the position of the current page in an ordered list of peer pages, such as a carousel or onboarding, and moves between them. Center it below the pages. More than about ten dots are hard to count at a glance; for longer lists, prefer a grid. It follows the iOS 26 kit Page control on every screen: 8px dots 8px apart in a 24px capsule, with a 44px target on a phone. Tap the leading or trailing side of the current dot for the previous or next page; with a mouse, click a dot. Drag across the dots to scrub, or past either end to reach the first or last page. Scroll the pages without animation while scrubbing, as details.scrubbing tells, and with reduced motion, as motion-reduce:scroll-auto does here. From seven pages the dots past a window around the current page shrink to 6px and 4px, suggesting more pages, and the rest hide, as the kit variants show. The capsule behind the dots shows while a pointer presses or scrubs with the automatic background, always with prominent, for a page control that is the main navigation of the screen, and never with minimal, which also turns off scrubbing since it gives no feedback.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: SegmentedControl provides two visual variants: segmented (default) with a sliding background highlight, and underline with an animated line indicator under the active tab and no background container. flush makes the underline indicator match the text width exactly, with gap between tabs instead of padding, and block stretches the tabs evenly across the container. orientation="vertical" stacks the tabs: the thumb slides up and down, and the underline becomes a line on the left side, for sidebar-style navigation. Both variants take the full 9-step size scale of Button, Input, Select and SelectControl, which sets the height, font size, icon size and spacing of the tabs. icon on a tab puts an icon before its label, sized to the size; leave out the label for icon-only tabs of a horizontal control and give each an aria-label. Vertical tabs keep their labels, so the example offers no icon only there: they are a list, a sidebar or on a phone an inset grouped list, and a list row always has a title. badge takes a number or an object with content, color, variant and pill, shown after the label inside the control; a count names what it counts, so it sits on a labelled tab and icon-only tabs carry none. disabled affects the whole group, which on a phone shows at half opacity when horizontal, as a disabled iOS segmented control does; monthDisabled disables only Month, whose label in a horizontal control on a phone takes the disabled label of iOS, 20% of the label color, while its row in a vertical one shows at half opacity. Arrow-key navigation skips disabled tabs without resetting the selected value.On a phone horizontal tabs of either variant are the iOS 27 segmented control, filling the row of a phone screen, in its two sizes. The default md and larger are the large control of iOS 27 apps, as Calendar and Reminders draw it and SwiftUI draws a segmented Picker in a toolbar: a 48px glass capsule, a 40px gray selection 4px inside it, 8px between segments, every label 15px Medium and primary. sm and smaller are the small one, the plain control of SwiftUI's Picker in content and of Safari's bookmarks: a 32px capsule of the tertiary fill, a white selection 2px inside it, labels 13px, Semibold when selected. mobileMaterial switches the look, as for Button: flat makes the large one plain, 49px as SwiftUI's .controlSize(.large), and glass puts the small one under the Liquid Glass of .glassEffect(). Inside a phone Toolbar every control is the large glass one. The phone example puts the control in a top bar, where it holds the bar alone, in a bottom bar, or above the content, as Safari's bookmarks do, over a day of events under the glass of the bars; placement picks one. Vertical tabs of either variant are an inset grouped list, as iOS lists a choice: 52px rows with the 17px label and a checkmark on the selected row instead of the thumb. A segment with an icon and a label shows the icon alone, at the 20px symbol size, as UISegmentedControl draws an action with a title and an image; the label stays the segment's accessible name, since iOS segments carry a title or a symbol, not both. They carry no badges either: on a phone (below 768px with touch.css, or in a phone layout) a badge is not drawn and its count stays in the segment's accessible name, so write a count into the label to show it. A page that is only narrow, without touch.css, keeps its badges. mobileSegmentWidth sets the segments' widths, as UISegmentedControl does: equal, the default, gives every segment the widest one's width, and content gives each its label and the same air around it, a compact control. At the control's own width the widest label stands 4px inside its segment in the large control and 9px in the small one, as iOS 27.2 sets them. Underline tabs draw the same segmented control on a phone and every control there is a capsule filling its row, so the phone view has no variant, flush, block, pill and badge controls, and its size offers sm and md.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: On Phone, put a select in a Field row of a FieldGroup, as the Forms: Settings do: the value and its up-down chevrons sit at the row's end, like an iOS pop-up button, and its list opens over the value, as the pop-up menu of an iOS picker does: 250px wide, its end at the chevron's end, 9px below the row's top, and toward the larger part of the screen. The value is hidden under the list while it is open. The list is an iOS menu, so its rows are the rows of Menu › On a phone: a description is the row's subtitle, and so is a tooltip; the checkmark leads every row whatever checkPosition says, and "none" still leaves it out, so the Overview's Phone view offers "start" and "none" and the other Phone previews leave out that control. It has no search, as an iOS menu has none: a long list scrolls. A clearable select with its default trigger has no clear button there, as an iOS pop-up button has none (a custom trigger owns its clearing): its list leads with a None row in a section of its own, checked while nothing is chosen, and choosing it unsets the value and closes the list, a multiple one too, as Reminders does. noneLabel names the row. On an Android phone a press opens Android's choice dialog instead of the list, as a value row of an Android settings screen does: the field's label as its title (title sets another), a row with a radio for each option, and Cancel. A press on a row chooses it and closes the dialog; Cancel, Escape or a press outside change nothing. picker="menu" keeps the list. A multiple select keeps the list unless picker="dialog" asks for the dialog: a checkbox in each row, and OK applies them, as in the Notifications example of the Forms: Settings. Pass the selection as value: a string, or an array of strings with multiple. multiple also changes how onChange and TriggerView are typed: onChange receives the selected option, or every selected option, and TriggerView receives {"{ values, selectedAll }"}. The trigger is a SelectControl: variant, size (the 9-step scale of Button, Input, SelectControl and SegmentedControl), pill and dropdownIconType style it. block stretches it across its container, here the 290px field, and the list takes its width. Without block the trigger fits its value and the list is at least listMinWidth, here 240px, wider than the trigger, so align places it against the trigger. side is the side the list prefers. checkPosition puts the checkmark at the start or the end of a row; "none" leaves the column out. clearable adds a clear action. loading shows loadingPlaceholder and keeps the list closed. disabled disables the select, and a disabled select is not submitted with its form. opticallyAlign offsets the trigger by its gutter: "start" puts the text of a ghost trigger on the label's edge, and "end" puts the end of a block one, its indicator, on the field's end. A framed trigger keeps its gutter, so the example offers the setting for ghost only, and "end" only with block: a narrower trigger does not reach the field's end. On Phone the select is the value of a row in a FieldGroup, with {"block={false}"} and align="end". The row sets its height, insets, type and colors, and the list opens over the value with the checkmark leading. So the Phone preview has no variant, size, pill, block, dropdownIconType, side, align and opticallyAlign controls, and its checkPosition is "start" or "none": the checkmark leads every row, and "none" leaves it out. A clearable select leads its list with a None row instead of a clear button.

examples.name: With descriptions
examples.details: Options carrying a description field render a secondary line under each label. The title stays semibold in every state (idle, highlighted, selected). The component handles that automatically, no optionClassName needed. Use TriggerStartIcon to reflect the selected option's identity in the trigger. In a phone row the value stands alone at the row's end, so the row has no trigger icon.

All selects are searchable by default, but will only present a searchbox when it makes sense. Currently, this means when there are more than 15 options. On a phone the list is an iOS menu, which has no search: a long list scrolls.

examples.name: Select Control
examples.details: Use variant to stylize the control: its styles are like those of {""}, with the small differences of {""}, and ghost has no frame. size sets the control's height, font size, gutter and the placement of its icon and indicator, on the 9-step scale of Button, Input, Select and SegmentedControl; pill rounds it fully and widens its gutter, and its clear action is a pill too. StartIcon puts an icon before the value, sized, spaced and colored by the control, and dropdownIconType picks the indicator. selected says the control holds a value and turns off the placeholder styling. It does nothing to the content, which is up to you, so here it follows the value: pick a period, or clear it. Pass onClearClick to make the control clearable: the clear action shows while it is selected. During loading the dropdown icon and clear action are hidden, the control is marked aria-busy and it ignores pointer and keyboard interaction; add disabled to dim it as well. invalid marks the control invalid; pair it with the field's errorMessage. disabled disables it both visually and accessibly. block stretches it across its container, here the 290px field. opticallyAlign offsets the control by its gutter: "start" puts the start of a ghost control, its icon or its text, on the label's edge, and "end" puts the end of a block one, its indicator, on the field's end. A framed control keeps its gutter, so the example offers the setting for ghost only, and "end" only with block: a narrower control does not reach the field's end. The control's own aria-labelledby names it by the label and the value, as Select's trigger is named.On Phone the control is the value of a row in a FieldGroup: the value and its up-down chevrons sit at the row's end, as an iOS pop-up button. The row sets its height, insets, type and colors, so the Phone preview has no variant, size, pill, StartIcon, dropdownIconType, block and opticallyAlign controls. A selected value takes the secondary label color (the primary one in a group with columns), a placeholder the tertiary one. A clearable control unsets its value with the menu's None row, as iOS pop-ups do, rather than a clear button. A row has no frame to color, so the error is the row's errorMessage line.

To decide when the control opens (or to keep it closed), pass onInteract and control the dropdown's open state yourself: the wrapping trigger then no longer opens on its own.

components.description: "A navigation sidebar for an app shell that folds to an icon rail and becomes a drawer on a phone."

props.description: Visual variant

props.description: Which side the sidebar is on

props.name: pill
props.description: Rows as capsules: their ends move 16px in (from 12) so text and icons keep clear of the round ends. A tree moves every level by the same 4px, so a nested row stays under its parent's text; other rows keep the axis of the rows over them and of the folded rail's icons, and only their end moves in. Set pill on the controls in the sidebar as well (SegmentedControl, Input, Button)

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: The examples use local ResponsiveSidebarProvider, ResponsiveSidebar and SidebarDemoPage helpers from Responsive composition. They keep the desktop rail and use the existing SidebarMobile drawer with a Page toolbar on phones. The mobile presentation is a navigation adaptation, not an iPad sidebar squeezed into a phone. Use variant for the look of the whole shell: "app" is the sidebar of a product, 260px, pill rows on a grey ground and a page with no inset. collapsible sets how the sidebar folds, to an icon rail or off the canvas, and open folds it (or press ⌘B). Rows keep their place as it folds, the labels fade, and along the rail the next tooltip opens at once. labelSize sets the group labels, icons the icons of the rows (a sidebar without them does not fold to a rail). badges puts a Badge in SidebarMenuBadge: it sits as far from the row's edge as from its top and bottom, its digits end where plain counts and the chevron end, and in the folded rail it becomes a dot of its color above the icon. submenus turns Settings into a row with a submenu: a SidebarMenuItem whose SidebarMenuSub holds the next level; expanded on the item turns its SidebarMenuChevron and open on the submenu shows it. Set --sidebar-menu-sub-max-height to a submenu's real height for an even fold. search adds a SidebarInput, an Input with a search icon that takes every Input prop, and narrows the rows to the ones that match. footer holds a dismissible SidebarCard or a person row whose Menu opens above it; the person row is 40px tall, so the round end of its highlight is concentric with the avatar on the icons' axis. bordered sets the inset page of the default variant against a flat one. On a phone the toolbar opens the same navigation tree in a full-screen drawer, so the Phone view leaves out collapsible, open and labelSize.

examples.name: Tree
examples.details: A tree of screens of any depth in SidebarMenuSub tree. A group row starts with SidebarMenuChevron placement="start" in place of an icon and folds on a press anywhere on it, its chevron turned down while open (aria-expanded on the row); a leaf shows its icon in the same 24px cell. Each level (indent) is one cell further in, so the text starts at 36, 60 and 84px and a nested row's chevron or icon stands right under its parent's text. Where groups have an icon of their own (a folder), put the chevron before it and give leaves SidebarMenuChevron placement="start" blank. The search narrows the rows to the ones that match and opens the groups that hold a match; the button beside it expands or collapses every level.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: On Phone, each slider stands in a cell of a grouped list, as in iOS Settings: the group's title names the slider and the slider fills the cell. One value ends the cell, a field the number can be typed in, a range goes under the track, and with marks the cell shows the scale instead of a value. Set range and give value two numbers for a range, or three or more for several thumbs; onChange then receives an array. step is how far a drag or a key moves the value at a time: 25 here stops it on the marks. A typed number is taken as it is, whole and within the scale. minStepsBetweenThumbs keeps the thumbs that many steps apart. resetValue, with one thumb, adds a button to the label that brings the value back; a disabled slider leaves that button out. unit follows the value and prefixUnit comes before it. marks label points of the scale under the track, horizontal only. trackColor and rangeColor color the track and its fill. startAdornment and endAdornment stand at the ends of a horizontal track, as Settings puts a small and a large letter at the ends of a text size slider; on a phone they take the place of the value. They are decoration, so the slider's name has to say what it sets. A label given as JSX can carry a tooltip, and orientation="vertical" stands the slider up. On a phone the slider is horizontal, as a list of iOS settings has no vertical slider, and a tooltip opens on hover, which a phone does not have, so the Phone preview leaves out those controls. The value at the end of the cell is a field: a tap brings up the number pad and the typed number moves the slider, taken as the slider's own field takes it, as Keynote for iPhone takes a value in the field next to its slider. The cell has no label row for a reset button, so the reset is a row of its own under the slider's group, its label centered in the accent, as Settings resets Hover Text's size; a disabled slider dims the row with it. A slider with a label of its own keeps the reset beside its value on a phone, as the small round gray button of the iOS 27 kit: a 28px circle that takes touches 44px around it. Marks take the place of the value, so with marks the phone shows no unit either.

examples.name: In a settings group

On a phone the group's title names it, one cell of the row's height holds the track and its value, typed in place as in the Overview, and the group's footer says what the setting does. A reset that changes nothing only crowds the group, so here it is the heading's action, the tinted text at the end of an iOS list's header: it shows once the value differs from its default, brings the default back and goes. The heading keeps its height either way, so the list does not move. On a desktop the slider keeps its label, its value and its round reset.

examples.details: Every direct child is an item, in the order of value. A row drags from anywhere but a control, so the switch keeps working. Its grip is hidden and still takes the keyboard: Tab to the row and press the arrow keys. On a touch screen a row lifts after a short hold, and a swipe still scrolls the page. Esc cancels a drag. examples.name: Overview
examples.details: A tip teaches a feature people might not find on their own: a title that names it and a sentence or two on how to use it. Show one tip at a time, close to what it explains, and stop showing it once the feature is used or the tip is closed. A tip is not for errors or for news about a task: use an Alert or a Toast. It follows the TipKit kit, the macOS Mini Tip on a desktop and on a phone the shape TipKit's tip and most of Apple's own cards share, on the card of a grouped list or, for a popover tip, in the iOS 27 alert's glass. Apple's apps also draw cards of their own, with a large image, a centered layout or capsule buttons; build those from a Card and Buttons. An inline tip takes its place in the layout. A symbol in icon leads the message in the secondary color; onClose shows Close in the trailing corner. On a phone the tip is the opaque card of a grouped list, so place it on a grouped background. actions sit side by side below the message, each as wide as the others; use small pill buttons, as the kit does. On a phone each action is a row of text in its color under a separator, one under another, starting under the text, as iOS cards show them. With mobileActions="buttons" each action is a capsule as wide as the tip: on iOS TipKit's mini tip, a 50px capsule with a 17px Semibold label in the action's color (the accent for a primary one) on that color at 8% over a light gray, the tip 22px from its top to the title, 4px from the title to the message and 22px from the words to the action; the Android look keeps each Button's color and variant. Use it for a card that asks for a permission, with one soft primary button. It changes nothing on a desktop, so only the Phone preview offers it, and only with actions. With arrowEdge the tip points at what it explains with the kit's arrow, centered on that edge, and leaves room for the arrow on that side. On a phone the tip stands over or under its control, as TipKit's inline tip does: no iOS screen sets a control beside a card of a grouped list, so the Phone preview offers no sideways arrow.

components.name: Toast
components.description: "A brief notification that gives feedback on an action, with an optional description and action button."

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: Render <Toaster /> once near the root of your app, then call toast(...) from any handler. PlexUI renders toasts and manages their interaction while sonner supplies the toast store. Its full API (toast.promise, toast.loading, toast.dismiss, toast.custom) is re-exported as-is. Call toast with a message, or toast.success, .error, .warning and .info for the semantic types, which map to PlexUI's success, danger, warning and info tokens. Each of them shows its icon; icon: null leaves it out, and icon takes an element of your own instead. No richColors is passed, so the types retheme with data-theme. The options add a description under the message, an action button and a cancel one (either closes the toast after its onClick), and closeButton. toast.promise ties one toast to an async operation: it shows a loading state, then swaps to success or error, and takes the same options; here saveProfile() resolves with {"{ name: \"Profile\" }"} after 1.5 seconds. Spread compact into the options for a centered toast: on a desktop a toast shrinks to its content anyway, and on a phone, where a toast fills the width, a compact one keeps the width of its content. duration: Infinity keeps a toast open until the user closes it, so give it a labelled action or a close button: a way to close it from the keyboard. An error that waits like this is an alert (see Screen readers). On a desktop the message and its controls share a row: the buttons stand 16px after the message and 8px apart, small 28px buttons with 6px corners (the action solid, the cancel soft), and the close button is the same 28px button, plain, at the end. With a description the buttons go under the message, at the end, and the close button stays on the title's line. On a phone a toast is as wide as its message and stands in the middle, a glass capsule as the system's own message at the top of an iPhone, 24px corners once it has a description, with 15pt text, with its buttons drawn as a medium phone Button, a 34px capsule in a 44px target. One button stands at the end of the message's row, where a banner shows its time, and the message wraps in its own column; a cancel and an action together stand under the message, and so does a button that would leave the message less than 8em. Under 600px a long message wraps at 14px gutters past the safe area. A toast with rich colors keeps its color.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: A toggle group sets several on or off choices that belong together, where any number may be on, such as the days an alarm repeats on. For one choice out of several, use a SegmentedControl or a RadioGroup; for a single setting, a Switch or a Checkbox. Round items spread across their row are the weekday buttons of the iOS Clock app's Repeat row, as in Add Alarm. On a phone with touch.css each is a 35pt circle with its letter at 17pt Semibold, as the native ones are. A narrow letter alone does not name a day: give each item the day's full name with aria-label. The summary beside the label is the app's to write; here it reads as the Clock app's does. The group's color fills a pressed item, a solid button; an item that is not pressed stays a soft secondary button whatever the color. size sizes every item as it sizes a Button, from 3xs (22px) to 3xl (48px). pill rounds the items fully, circles here, as uniform makes them as wide as they are tall, for a letter or an icon. block spreads them across the width of their container; without it the group is as wide as its items, 8px apart. disabled disables the whole group. On a phone with touch.css every item is fully rounded, as iOS draws its buttons, and a letter is the Clock app's 35pt circle at every size, so the Phone preview offers neither pill nor size. Items of text there take the three iOS button heights.

components.description: "The top and bottom bars of a phone screen: navigation, a title, a search field and actions over the content."

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: Toolbar is a phone component: under 768px it renders, from 768px up it takes no space. Each example shows the phone view. Leading and trailing items take 44px targets; an inline title is centered across the whole width. titleStyle sets the size and place of the title: inline in the row of controls, large on a row of its own below them (on a page it stands at the top of the content and scrolls with it, overscroll included; once it has gone under the controls, they show it inline), and compact-large or compact-medium at the leading edge of the row, on a screen with no Back button. subtitle adds a second line under an inline or large title. titleAlign="start" puts an inline title after the leading items. Scroll the content: the bar's background meets the rows under it, and the glass starts to cast a shadow. Toolbar.Group puts related actions in one capsule; a single action, as Back or Close, keeps a capsule of its own. Without Toolbar.Title the bar holds its controls alone. A ButtonGroup in a toolbar is the same capsule. Name each icon button with aria-label. Toolbar.Content fill stretches a search field across the row in the place of the title, up to the trailing items; the field takes the row height and the material of the bar buttons. That is the open search: until a tap opens it, the search waits in a field across a row under the controls (search row) or behind a Search button in the bar (search button), and Close puts it back, as iOS 27.2 raises the field of the bar's drawer into the bar and hides the title and the buttons; a segmented row stays under the open field. A Search button can open its field at the bottom instead (field bottom), as SwiftUI's search button opens it over the keyboard: the field and Close take a bottom bar of their own, the top bar's title and buttons go, and a segmented row moves up in their place. Toolbar.Row adds a row under the controls, part of the bar: a SegmentedControl that switches the screen's views, as a chat list shows its folders under its bar, or a search field. It spans the bar between its gutters, 10px under the controls, and the bar's background and line take it in. Several rows stand in their order, 10px apart: a search field over a segmented control, as iOS 27.2 sets them under the search field of a bar's drawer. A segmented control in it is glass at its default size, as a chat list draws its folders under its bar in iOS 27: a 40px capsule, the gray selection 34px and 3px inside it, 15px labels 12px from their segments' ends. It fills the row: its segments share the width and scroll when they do not fit, and a badge is not drawn, its count staying in the segment's accessible name. size="sm" gives the small plain one (32px, as iOS 27.2 draws a segmented Picker under a bar) and size="lg" the large glass one (48px). A search field in it is the bar's: 44px of glass. Under a large title on a page the rows stand under the title at the top of the content, 16px under its baseline; scrolled up to the bar they stay pinned under its controls, and the bar's background, edge and line reach under them, as iOS 27.2 pins them. placement="bottom" sets the bar at the bottom of the page with 48px targets and the device's bottom safe area. Toolbar.Content centers a main action; with fill a search field or a single action takes the whole row. The 48px items stand 28px from the sides and above the home indicator, 12px apart, whatever the background: iOS 27.2 keeps them in place over every scroll edge, and a band (glass or hard) only starts 10px above them. A search field holds SearchSm, set in Regular; a plus next to it takes iconSize="sm", as Contacts draws it smaller than the other symbols. The page content scrolls under both bars. A screen holds one search field, so with one in the top bar the bottom bar offers neither its own field nor its Search button. background sets how a bar meets the content scrolled under it. glass, the default of a top bar, is a translucent, blurred bar with a hairline. soft, the default of a bottom bar, is the scroll edge effect of iOS 26 and draws no line: once content is under a top bar with a title, a blur hides it under the controls and lets go of it past the bar, under a thin veil of the canvas color (iOS 27.2: 55% at the top, 20% at the bar's bottom, none 24px below), while a top bar of controls alone on a page covers only the status bar, and once content runs on under a bottom bar on a page, a blur hides it under the controls behind a veil of the canvas color that grows toward the screen's edge, with no band and no line (iOS 27.2: none 34px above the items, 15% at their top, 46% from 43px into them); each glass control stands out over it. A Sheet's bottom bar fades its content into the panel. hard is an opaque bar of the canvas color with a hairline. blur has no fill and no line: the content under the bar is blurred a little over the bar and past it, and heavily toward the screen's edge. Glass, hard and blur show themselves once content is under the bar: under the top bar after the content has scrolled, over the bottom bar while it continues below. Page.Header, Page.Footer, the bars of a Sheet and TabBar take the same values. The top and the bottom bar each take their own; the bottom bar's controls stand under the preview.

  <Toolbar.Title subtitle="24 orders">Orders</Toolbar.Title> {/* a subtitle with an inline or large title */}
  <Toolbar.Trailing>
    <Button color="secondary" variant="soft" uniform pill aria-label="More"><DotsHorizontal /></Button>
  </Toolbar.Trailing>
  <Toolbar.Row>
    <Input
      type="search"
      variant="soft"
      pill
      placeholder="Search"
      aria-label="Search orders"
      startAdornment={<SearchSm />}
      value={query}
      onChange={(evt) => setQuery(evt.target.value)}
      onClear={() => setQuery("")}
    />
  </Toolbar.Row>

<Page.Content>...</Page.Content>

examples.details: A search field under the title is a row of the bar: Toolbar.Row holding an Input with type="search" and variant="soft" pill, the bar's magnifier, text and placeholder in a glass capsule. Under a large title the row starts the content, the field 16px under the title's baseline and the list 10px under the field; scroll it up and the title goes under the bar while the field pins under the controls, 10px under them, as iOS 27.2 pins the search field of a large title. With an inline or compact title, which the controls switch, the row stands in the bar from the start. With onClear the field shows the filled clear circle of iOS while it holds text, in place of the browser's own clear button. Outside a bar, as at the top of a sheet's content, the same Input stands in the content and scrolls with it.

  <Toolbar.Content fill search> {/* "auto"; or search="top", search="bottom" */}
    <Input
      variant="soft"
      pill
      placeholder="Search"
      aria-label="Search orders"
      startAdornment={<SearchSm />}

      onClear={() => setQuery("")}
    />
  </Toolbar.Content>

examples.details: search on Toolbar.Content marks the screen's search field and sets where it stands. Write the field once, in the bottom bar. "bottom" keeps it there, in reach of the thumb, as iOS 26 places a screen's search. "top" turns it into a search button, first among the top bar's trailing actions and in one capsule with the icon buttons beside it. Pressed, the field grows out of the button to the bar's end, the title and the actions fade, and the leading action becomes a back arrow; the bottom bar, which held only the field, leaves its place. Back or Escape closes the search, clears the field and gives the focus back to the button. "auto", or search alone, is the platform's place: the bottom on iOS, the top in the Plex Android look. The button takes the field's aria-label as its name. In the Plex Android look the open field is a 46px pill of the bar's glass from 58px (the gutter, the back circle and the gap) to 6px from the screen's edge, its text 17px with the hint in a light gray, and it opens over 380ms. In a Sheet the sheet stands at the full screen, with no corners, while the search is open, its bar 5px under the status bar and 6px from the sides, and settles back as the search closes.

examples.name: Overview
examples.details: Tooltips provide supplementary information on hover or keyboard focus. Touch-only users need visible helper text or a tap-triggered Popover. The Overview uses pointer and keyboard interactions, so it has no separate Phone preview. For copying, Copy Tooltip confirms the action after a successful tap. Any element can be the trigger: trigger shows text, a button and an icon button. Text is no tab stop of its own, so wrap it in Tooltip.TriggerDecorator, which makes it one and marks it with a dotted underline; a plain span shows its tooltip on hover only, and a keyboard never reaches it. An icon button names itself with aria-label, and its tooltip says the same in words. compact is for short tooltips of one to three words: little padding (2px by 8px) and inverted colors, a dark fill with light text in the light theme and the other way round in the dark one. side is the side the tooltip prefers; it turns to the other side when there is no room. A disabled button can tell why in its tooltip on hover (a disabled button is no tab stop): pass the reason as content while it is disabled. To show a tooltip only under a condition, pass null otherwise.
